newsitem.title: USA: Albright reaffirms tough U.S. policy toward Iraq.
newsitem.headline: Albright reaffirms tough U.S. policy toward Iraq.

text.p: Secretary of State Madeleine Albright on Wednesday reaffirmed the hardline U.S. policy toward Iraq as long as President Saddam Hussein is in power and warned that a U.N. oil-for-food programme could end if Baghdad did not live up to its promises.

But in a speech to Georgetown University, where she once taught international relations, she also outlined the new dialogue Washington is prepared to begin immediately with Baghdad if a new, more peaceful government comes to power.

"If past is prologue, under the current government an Iraq released from sanctions and scrutiny would pick up where it left off half a dozen years ago -- before the mother of all coalitions stoppped it dead in its tracks," Albright said in a prepared text.

"For these reasons, our policy will not change," she said. "To those who ask how long our determination will last, how long we will oppose Iraqi intransigence, how long we will insist that the international community's standards be met, our answer is -- as long as it takes.
"The evidence is overwhelming that Saddam Hussein's intentions will never be peaceful," she said.

Albright, who led the U.S. charge against Iraq as U.N. ambassador from 1993 to last January, signalled that this resolve remains unshaken with her in her new post as America's top diplomat. But she also made clear there could be a change in U.S. policy including efforts to ease Iraq's re-integration into the world economy if Iraq had a change of government .

"Clearly, a change in Iraq's government could lead to a change in U.S. policy. Should that occur, we would stand ready, in coordination with our allies and friends, to enter rapidly into a dialogue with the successor regime," she said.
The dialogue would have two goals. First, to verify that the new Iraq would be "independent, unified and free from undue external influence for example, from Iran," she said.
Second, the United States would require "improvements in behaviour," such as compliance with U.N. resolutions relating to the Gulf War and respect for human rights.

"If our concerns were addressed satisfactorily, Iraq would no longer threaten regional security. Its isolation would end (and) the international community ... would look for ways to ease Iraq's re-integration," she said.

Albright insisted Saddam's power "rests on an increasingly narrow foundation of intimidation and terror" and she rejected suggestions that he had extended his control to northern Iraq after his troops entered the region last August when Kurdish groups were involved in a civil war.
She said the United States "will continue to support the establishment of a coherent and united Iraqi opposition which represents the country's ethnic and confessional diversity."
